newsitem.title: FRANCE: G7 backs peaceful end to Peru hostage crisis.
newsitem.headline: G7 backs peaceful end to Peru hostage crisis.

text.p: The Group of Seven industrialised nations and Russia on Friday backed Peru's efforts to end its 10-day hostage crisis without bloodshed and said that, as a general principle, no concession should be made to terrorism.

The G7 countries, in a statement issued by France which holds the group's rotating presidency, "expressed their solidarity with the Peruvian government and support its efforts to resolve the crisis peacefully, with the main objective of sparing human lives."

A French Foreign Ministry spokeswoman said the ambassadors of the G7 countries and Russia in Lima met on Thursday to discuss the siege of the Japanese ambassador's residence where Marxist guerrillas are holding more than 100 hostages to demand the release of jailed colleagues.
The statement "reaffirmed the general principle under which no concession must be made in the face of a terrorist action," a wording which appeared to leave some room for negotiation.

It said the Lima attack could not be justified by any political or ideological motive and the G7 countries were "prepared, individually and collectively, to help the Peruvian government by all the appropriate means that it could request."

Japan said earlier that it was consulting fellow G7 members Britain, Canada, France, Germany, Italy and the United States and was also in touch with Russia to try to work out a solution to the crisis.

"It is clear that the international community should not condone terrorism. It is also necessary for the international community to act as one to help resolve this crisis by setting free all the hostages peacefully and at an early date," Japanese Foreign Minister Yukihido Ikeda said.
Russian President Boris Yeltsin wrote to G7 leaders and Peruvian President Alberto Fujimori this week, calling for a collective G7 approach to the crisis.

He suggested a joint declaration offering coordinated moves including possible dispatch of anti-terrorist squads and establishment of a joint headquarters to conduct a hostage-freeing operation in Lima.
The crisis erupted on December 17 when the heavily-armed Tupac Amaru guerrillas stormed the Lima residence of the Japanese ambassador during a packed reception.
At the annual summit of G7 leaders in Lyon, France, last July, the world's seven most industrialised nations approved a list of 25 practical measures to defeat terrorism.

The package included pledges to reinforce police cooperation and training, share intelligence, make extradition procedures easier, cut off sources of terrorist funding and weapons and strengthen national anti-terrorism legislation.

Asked if Lima could be the first test of collective anti-terrorist moves by the G7 and Russia, which attended the Lyon summit as an observer, Japanese Foreign Ministry spokesman Hiroshi Hashimoto said it would depend on discussions among members.
"At this point it is too early to say what specific measures could be taken," he said. "In either case, there is no change in Japan's position of complete support for President Fujimori."
